title: 📘 UNIT 3: PEOPLES AND STATES IN ETHIOPIA AND THE HORN TO THE END OF 13TH C.
notes: 🌍 Ethiopia and the Horn of Africa are characterized by great linguistic, religious, cultural and ethnic diversity.

title: 📌 3.1 LANGUAGES, RELIGIONS AND PEOPLES OF ETHIOPIA AND THE HORN
notes:
🌍 Ethiopia and the Horn have over 80 languages with many dialects.

⭐ The languages belong mainly to two super-families:
• Afro-Asiatic
• Nilo-Saharan

🧩 Despite linguistic and cultural diversity, there is strong unity among the peoples.

title: 🗣️ 3.1.1 LANGUAGE FAMILIES
notes:
🌐 Ethiopia and the Horn have two major language super-families:

1️⃣ Afro-Asiatic
2️⃣ Nilo-Saharan

title: 🌐 AFRO-ASIATIC LANGUAGE FAMILY
notes:
The Afro-Asiatic super-family includes:

• Cushitic
• Semitic
• Omotic

title: 🟢 CUSHITIC LANGUAGES
notes:
⭐ Cushitic has several branches:

• North Cushitic: mainly Beja

• Central Cushitic: Bilen and Agaw languages

• Eastern Cushitic: the largest and most diverse branch

title: 🛐 3.1.2 MAJOR RELIGIONS OF ETHIOPIA
notes:
⭐ Major religions:

• Indigenous religions
• Judaism
• Christianity
• Islam

title: 🌿 INDIGENOUS RELIGION
notes:
• Native beliefs practiced within particular cultures.

• Followers believe in a Supreme Being and revere ancestors.

• Natural phenomena may be considered sacred.

title: 🌿 OROMO WAQEFFANNA
notes:
• Oromo Waqeffanna recognizes Waqa as the Supreme Being.

• Qallu (male) and Qallitti (female) act as spiritual functionaries.

• Mixing indigenous beliefs with Christianity or Islam is called syncretism.

title: ✡️ JUDAISM
notes:
• Practiced in Ethiopia from ancient times according to historical sources.

• Followed by the Bete-Israel (House of Israel).

• Historically concentrated mainly in northern Ethiopia.

• Shares several Old Testament traditions and practices with Ethiopian Orthodox Christianity.

title: ✝️ CHRISTIANITY IN ETHIOPIA
notes:
• Introduced around 330 AD by Frumentius (Freminatos).

• He converted King Ezana and his close associates.

• Christianity gained royal support and became the state religion.

title: ⛪ SPREAD OF CHRISTIANITY
notes:
• The Nine Saints helped spread Christianity from the late 5th century.

• Churches and monasteries were established, including Debre-Damo.

• The Bible was translated into Ge'ez.

title: 📖 CHRISTIAN CENTERS AND FIGURES
notes:
⭐ Important Christian centers included:
• Lalibela
• Debra-Bizan
• Debra-Hayiq
• Debre-Libanos
• Others

⭐ Important religious figures included:
• Abba Iyesus Moa
• Abba Giyorgis Zegasicha
• Abune Tekle-Haymanot

title: ☪️ ISLAM IN ETHIOPIA
notes:
• Islam arose in Arabia in the early 7th century.

• Muslim refugees first came to Aksum in 615 AD.

• King Armah Ella Seham (Al-Nejashi) gave them asylum from 615–628 AD.

title: 🕌 SPREAD OF ISLAM
notes:
• Islam later spread peacefully through trade routes.

• Three main gateways: Red Sea, Gulf of Aden and Indian Ocean.

• Zeila became an important gateway into the Ethiopian interior.

title: 🌍 AREAS OF ISLAMIC EXPANSION
notes:
Islam spread into:

• Harar
• Shewa
• Wollo
• Bale
• Arsi
• Hadiya
• Somali regions

⭐ Muslim sultanates emerged along major trade routes.

title: 🏘️ 3.1.3 SETTLEMENT PATTERN OF PEOPLES OF ETHIOPIA
notes: 📍 Settlement pattern means the distribution of peoples across the landscape.

title: 🔄 PEOPLING OF ETHIOPIA
notes:
Peopling of Ethiopia resulted from long-term population movements caused by:

• Push factors: shortage of resources

• Pull factors: availability of resources

title: 🌍 FACTORS INFLUENCING SETTLEMENT
notes:
⭐ Settlement patterns were influenced by:

• Environmental factors
• Socioeconomic factors
• Political factors

title: 🗺️ DISTRIBUTION OF PEOPLES
notes:
• Cushitic and Semitic speakers historically occupied areas between the Red Sea and Blue Nile before dispersing.

• Cushitic speakers are the main linguistic group, followed by Semitic speakers.

title: 🌿 OMOTIC AND NILOTIC PEOPLES
notes:
• Most Omotic peoples live in southwestern Ethiopia along the Omo River valley.

• Nilotic-speaking peoples mainly live along the Ethiopia–Sudan border.

• Some Chari-Nile groups settled as far as Southern Omo.

title: 🏺 3.2 PRE-AKSUMITE STATES AND THEIR GEOGRAPHICAL SETTING
notes: ⭐ Several states and centers existed before the rise of Aksum.

title: 🌍 PUNT
notes:
• Ancient state in the Horn of Africa.

• Exact location and boundaries are uncertain.

• Associated with coastal areas of present-day Djibouti, Eritrea, Ethiopia and Somalia.

title: 🚢 PUNT: TRADE WITH EGYPT
notes:
• Had trade relations with Egypt from the 3rd millennium BC.

• Exported gold, ivory, animal skins, myrrh and ostrich feathers.

• Received items such as hatchets, daggers and necklaces from Egypt.

title: 🏛️ YEHA
notes:
• About 30 km northeast of Aksum.

• Presumably appeared around 1000 BC.

• Wealth peaked between 750 and 500 BC.

• Known for stone masonry, buildings, inscriptions and a temple.

title: 🪨 HAWULTI-MELAZO
notes:
• Located southeast of Aksum.

• Stone tablets with inscriptions were excavated there.

title: 👑 DAMAT
notes:
• Existed before the rise of Aksum.

• Center located a few kilometers south of Aksum.

• Rulers used the South Arabian political and religious title 'Mukarib'.

• Had relations with South Arabia.

• Used the Red Sea port of Adulis.

title: 📌 OTHER PRE-AKSUMITE CENTERS
notes:
Other pre-Aksumite centers included:

• Addi-Seglemeni
• Metera
• Kaskase
• Coloe

title: 👑 3.3 AKSUMITE KINGDOM
notes: 📍 Aksum emerged in the 1st century AD with its political and religious center at Aksum.

title: 🏛️ AKSUM: POLITICAL DEVELOPMENT
notes:
• Initially a small state.

• Expanded greatly during the 4th–6th centuries.

• Territory extended beyond the Red Sea into southern Arabia, west to the Abay, north to Eritrea and south toward Shewa.

title: 🌾 AKSUM: ECONOMY
notes:
• Plough agriculture was important.

• Tribute connected the king with the people.

• Local and international trade generated considerable income.

• Adulis was the major Red Sea trading port.

title: 🪙 AKSUM: COINS AND WRITING
notes:
• Bronze, silver and gold coins were minted.

• Ge'ez developed as a written language.

• Sabean and Greek were also used before Ge'ez became dominant.

title: ⛪ AKSUM: RELIGION
notes:
• Indigenous religions existed before Christianity.

• Christianity was introduced in the 4th century AD.

• Islam reached the region in the early 7th century.

title: 🏗️ AKSUM: ACHIEVEMENTS AND LEGACY
notes:
⭐ Major achievements included:

• Monolithic stelae and obelisks
• Temples and tombs
• Iron tools
• Bricks
• Coins
• Shipbuilding technology

🌍 Developed civilization centered around Aksum.

title: 📉 AKSUM: DECLINE
notes:
• Muslim Arab control of the Red Sea

• Destruction of Adulis in 702 AD

• Loss of international trade

• Decline of economic, political and military power

title: ⚔️ AKSUM: INTERNAL PROBLEMS
notes:
• Internal political disturbances and rebellions

• Loss of control over South Arabia

• Rebellion of the Beja people

• Aksum was gradually pushed southward and later became centered around areas inhabited by the Agaw.

title: ✝️ 3.3.1 CHRISTIANITY AND THE AKSUMITE KINGDOM
notes: Christianity became an important part of the Aksumite Kingdom after its introduction in the 4th century AD.

title: 👤 FRUMENTIUS (FREMINATOS)
notes:
• Introduced Christianity to Ethiopia around 330 AD.

• Converted King Ezana.

• Became the first bishop of the Ethiopian Church as Abuna Salam.

title: ⭐ CHRISTIANITY IN AKSUM
notes:
• Received royal support.

• Became the state religion.

• Strengthened Ethiopia's relationship with Egypt.

• Ge'ez became the language of the Church after the Bible was translated.

title: ⛪ THE NINE SAINTS
notes:
• Arrived toward the end of the 5th century.

• Helped spread Christianity among the wider population.

• Churches and monasteries were established.

title: 🏛️ 3.4 ZAGWE DYNASTY
notes: The Zagwe Dynasty was associated with the local Agaw ruling class of Lasta.

title: 👑 ZAGWE: ORIGIN
notes:
• Came from the local Agaw ruling class of Lasta.

• Founded around 1150 AD by Mera Tekle Haymnot.

• Capital established at Adefa (Roha), later called Lalibela.

• The rise of Zagwe represented a political power shift rather than the creation of a completely new kingdom.

title: 🌾 ZAGWE: ECONOMY
notes:
• Agriculture was the economic base.

• Trade provided additional income.

• Zeila was the main trade outlet.

• Dahlak Islands also served as an outlet.

title: 🏗️ ZAGWE: MAJOR ACHIEVEMENT
notes:
• Famous for monolithic rock-hewn churches.

• Eleven rock-hewn churches were constructed during the reign of Emperor Lalibela in the first half of the 13th century.

• Lalibela became an important center of learning and Christian culture.

title: 📉 ZAGWE: FALL
notes:
• Succession disputes among Zagwe princes.

• Rival princes often used force to settle succession.

• Opposition from Tigray and Amhara regions.

title: 📜 ANTI-ZAGWE PROPAGANDA
notes:
• Anti-Zagwe propaganda was connected with the legends of Queen of Sheba and King Solomon.

• Yekuno Amlak organized a movement against Zagwe rule.

title: ⚔️ YEKUNO AMLAK AND THE END OF ZAGWE
notes:
• He defeated Yetbarek, the last Zagwe king, in 1270 AD.

• Yekuno Amlak claimed descent from the last Aksumite king, Dil Naod, and restored the so-called Solomonic dynasty.

title: ☪️ 3.5 SULTANATE OF SHEWA
notes: 🌍 The spread of Islam in the Horn was followed by the emergence of Muslim states from the 9th century AD.

title: 🚢 ZEILA TRADE ROUTE
notes:
• Decline of northern Ethiopian trade followed Arab control of the Red Sea and destruction of Adulis.

• Zeila became an important port for southeastern Ethiopian trade.

• The Zeila route connected the coast with the rich interior.

• It also became a major gateway for Islam into the Horn.

title: 🏛️ SULTANATE OF SHEWA
notes:
• First Muslim sultanate established in 896 AD.

• Founders claimed descent from the Makhzunmite clan of southern Arabia.

• The dynasty became known as the Makhzunmite dynasty.

• Located in the hot lowland region on the left of the Awash River.

• Internal power struggles contributed to its decline.

title: 👑 IFAT SULTANATE
notes:
• Emerged south of Shewa.

• Founded by Umar Walasma in 1285 AD.

• Associated with the Walasma dynasty.

• Became the strongest Muslim sultanate in the region.

• Controlled much of the profitable Zeila trade route.

• Became a major rival of the Christian highland state.

title: ⚔️ MAIN SOURCE OF CONFLICT
notes:
• Competition for control of long-distance trade and trade routes.

• Christian and Muslim states competed for control of important trade networks.
